sbh4.1:1.18: The seven attentions begin from a specific qualified state. The practitioner has attained: *labdha-manaskāra*, cultivated *praśrabdhi* and *cittaikāgratā*, attention is *dṛṣṭi-sthira* (view-stable) and *khara* (forceful), object-resolve is *pariśrabdha* (relaxed), and the *śamatha-vipaśyanā* signs have been grasped. Roughly the late stages of the nine mental abidings (stages 7–8).
sbh4.1:2.10: Four kinds of mundane-path travelers: non-Buddhist meditators (the seven attentions are not exclusively Buddhist), Buddhists with dull faculties, those with only *śamatha* background and unripe wholesome roots, and bodhisattvas deliberately postponing *bodhi*. The seven attentions are accessible to anyone with the contemplative skill; jhāna-attainment doesn't itself imply Buddhist enlightenment.
sbh4.1:3.5: The mundane path's structural pattern is invariant: at each level, the practitioner sees the *grossness* of the lower and the *calmness* of the higher, and through that comparative recognition generates *vairāgya* that releases attachment to the lower and inclines the mind to the higher. The engine of the mundane path: comparative recognition driving release.
sbh4.1:5.4: The characteristic move of the entire seven-attention sequence: see the *grossness* of where you are; see the *calmness* of where you're going. The practitioner is not *willing* themselves into the first *dhyāna* — they are recognizing the actual qualitative difference, and that recognition produces the release of attachment that allows transition.
sbh4.1:8.3: Critical Yogācāra refinement: sense-pleasures are double. *Kleśa-kāma* is the defilement-aspect (the craving). *Vastu-kāma* is the substance-aspect (the objects themselves — sights, sounds, etc.). The practice of *kāma-vairāgya* is primarily directed at *kleśa-kāma*, not *vastu-kāma*. The ascetic is not trying to make the world go away; they are trying to make their craving for the world go away.
sbh4.1:10.8: The canonical *kāma-upamā* set (eight similes), found in MN 22 (Alagaddūpama) and MN 54 (Potaliya). Each simile makes a different point: skeleton (no real nourishment), piece of meat (cause of conflict), grass-torch (burns the hand), coal-pit (painful), venomous snake (deadly), dream (unreal), borrowed ornaments (must be returned), fruit on a tree (one falls trying to grasp). Asanga anchors his framework in the Buddha's own similes.
sbh4.1:12.13: Asanga reframes the four ascetic requisites — food, clothing, bedding, medicine — utilitarianly. Each is *not* a source of pleasure but a *counter-action to suffering*: food counters hunger, clothing counters cold/heat-and-shame, bedding counters fatigue, medicine counters illness. The Yogācāra version of the standard *paccavekkhana* (reflection on the four requisites).
sbh4.1:13.5: *Śruta-cintā-vyavakīrṇa* — mixed with hearing-and-thinking. This first attention is not yet pure *bhāvanā* (cultivation). The practitioner is still working with conceptual recognition of grossness and calmness. The threefold *prajñā* — *śrutamayī*, *cintāmayī*, *bhāvanāmayī* — is the standard sequence; the seven attentions begin with the first two and progressively replace them with the third.
sbh4.1:14.5: The transition from the first attention to the second is the transition from *cintā* (thinking) to *bhāvanā* (cultivation). The same grossness-calmness recognition is no longer being *thought through* but *resolved upon* and *cultivated*. The *adhimokṣa* is direct commitment without intervening discursive process.
sbh4.1:15.3: The third attention is the threshold-crossing. Up through the second attention, the practitioner has been *preparing*. At the third attention, *the path arises* — the first actual abandoning of desire-realm defilements happens. The name *prāvivekya* (from *viveka* — seclusion) marks that the practitioner is now *separating* from desire-realm defilements.
sbh4.1:16.9: The fourth attention manages emerging-jhāna-factors. As *prīti-sukha* characteristic of jhāna emerges, two failure-modes can derail: *styāna-middha* (sloth, sinking into bliss) and *auddhatya* (agitation, excitement). Remedies: *prasadanīya manaskāra* (inspiring) when sinking, *saṁvejanīya manaskāra* (uplifting) when drooping.
sbh4.1:17.11: One of the most psychologically sophisticated passages in classical Buddhist meditation literature. The fourth attention has produced apparent dispassion, but Asanga warns: this could be real dispassion or *suppressed* desire held by the meditation-state itself. The practitioner runs an experimental test: deliberately attend to an attractive sign and watch what the mind does. Real abandonment shows equanimity; false abandonment shows *sevanā-nimna/pravaṇa/prābhāra* — three escalating signs of inclination.
sbh4.1:17.13: *Vāri-vad dhṛtaṁ* — 'held like water.' The mind is currently dispassionate but only because the meditative apparatus is holding the desire back, like water held by a dam. Remove the dam, and the desire flows again. A diagnostic protocol for distinguishing real progress from suppressed defilement.
sbh4.1:18.10: *Complete provisional release*. The mind has fully disengaged from all desire-realm defilements through the attentions, but the *bīja* (seed) is not yet uprooted. The release is *tāvat-kālika* — time-bound. The precise definition of the difference between *laukika* (mundane) and *lokottara* (supramundane) liberation. A practitioner who reports 'I've gotten over my desire-realm cravings' has attained *prayoga-niṣṭha* — real but not final.
sbh4.1:19.3: The seventh attention *is* the first *dhyāna*. It is not a step *toward* first *dhyāna* — it is the attention *in* first *dhyāna*. The whole seven-attention sequence has been the staged transition; the seventh attention is arrival.
sbh4.1:20.4: The italicized phrase is the standard sutta-formulary description of the first *dhyāna*: 'with sense-pleasures secluded, with evil unwholesome dharmas secluded, with thought, with examination, with seclusion-born rapture-and-happiness, the first *dhyāna* with five factors' (MN 4 etc.). Asanga shows that the seven-attention sequence yields *exactly* the canonical first *dhyāna*.
sbh4.1:21.9: Three-grade abandonment: strong (*adhimātra*) defilements at the seclusion attention (3rd); middling at the delight-gathering attention (4th); mild (*mṛdu*) at the practice-culminating attention (6th). The middling grade is addressed during the work of attention 5 (examination). Progress is graduated, not binary.
sbh4.1:22.14: The functional reduction: the seven attentions can be re-grouped into four task-types — conforming (preparatory: 1+2), counter-action (3+6), inspiring (4), review (5). Potentially more usable for instruction than the seven-attention enumeration.
sbh4.1:23.2: The seven-attention structure is *invariant across all eight mundane-path transitions*: desire-realm→1st jhāna, 1st→2nd (gross: *vitarka-vicāra*), 2nd→3rd (gross: *prīti*), 3rd→4th (gross: *sukha*), 4th→space, space→consciousness, consciousness→nothingness, nothingness→bhavāgra. The single algorithm carries the practitioner from the desire-realm all the way to the peak of existence.
sbh4.1:24.12: At the 1st-to-2nd transition, what was previously recognized as *calm* (first *dhyāna*) is now recognized as *gross* relative to the second. The criterion is *vitarka-vicāra* — thought-and-examination, rendered here as *manojalpa* (mental-talking). The pattern is recursive: the same seven-attention sequence runs again at every transition.
